summary: Presents a framework for understanding authorization of Internet resources and services, and derives requirements for authorization protocols. It serves as the base requirements document for that work.

eli5.summary: Before a library lets you borrow a book, it checks if you are allowed. This explains the general idea of such permission checks on the Internet.

questions: how do multiple organizations authorize users
subtitle: Framework for authorizing users to access Internet resources and services

tldr.problem: Internet services need to decide whether a user should have access to a resource or service, and this decision often involves multiple organizations with different roles and agreements.
tldr.mechanism: The framework defines authorization entities (users, home organizations, service providers), message sequences for communicating authorization decisions, and the role of policies and trust relationships in making access decisions.
tldr.outcome: The framework provides a common vocabulary and architecture for designing authorization protocols, serving as the basis for subsequent work on protocol requirements and application examples.

today: RFC 2904 is an Informational document that has not been obsoleted or updated. It remains the foundational reference for understanding authorization architectures and policy frameworks in multi-domain Internet systems.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 2904 presents a framework for understanding authorization of Internet resources and services. It is part of a three-document set on authorization under the AAAarch Research Group that also includes authorization requirements and application examples. The framework aims to provide a common scheme and vocabulary for discussing authorization across Internet services.

The document assumes that users have already been authenticated (verified to be who they claim). Authorization is the next step: deciding what authenticated users are allowed to do. The framework applies across many scenarios: from a simple single-organization case (such as a dial-in network access server) to complex roaming situations (where a user's home organization and the service provider are different) to distributed services (where multiple service providers cooperate to deliver one service).
sections.eli5: After you prove who you are (authentication), the next question is whether you are allowed to do what you asked (authorization). This document explains how that permission-checking works, especially when different organizations are involved.

sections.title: Authorization Entities and Trust Relationships
sections.content:
The framework identifies the basic entities involved in authorization: a User who requests access, a User Home Organization (UHO) that has a relationship with the user and knows what the user is allowed to do, a Service Provider's AAA Server that makes authorization decisions based on agreements with the UHO, and Service Equipment that provides the actual service.

Bilateral agreements between these entities establish what users can and cannot do. For example, a user's home organization may say 'this user can access our service between 9 a.m. and 11 a.m. daily,' while the service provider may say 'we allow access for all UHO members except between 5 a.m. and 10 a.m. on Sundays.' Both rules must be satisfied.

Trust is necessary for authorization to work. Static trust relationships (such as shared secrets, certificate authorities, or Kerberos servers) are established between organizations. These static relationships are then used to create dynamic trust relationships during an authorization transaction, allowing the user to prove that their home organization approves their request.
sections.eli5: There are four main players: you, your home organization (like your employer), the service provider's decision-maker, and the service provider's equipment. They all have to agree you should get access, and they trust each other based on agreements they made in advance.

sections.title: Message Sequences and Architectures
sections.content:
The framework describes three authorization message sequences in the simplest case (single domain): the agent sequence, the pull sequence, and the push sequence.

In the agent sequence, the user sends a request to the AAA Server, which forwards it to the Service Equipment with instructions, the equipment acknowledges, and the server replies to the user. In the pull sequence, the user sends a request to the Service Equipment, which then queries the AAA Server for authorization, the server replies, and the equipment tells the user it is ready. In the push sequence, the user first gets a ticket or certificate from the AAA Server proving it is authorized, then sends that token along with its request to the Service Equipment.

These same sequences apply to roaming (where the user's home organization and service provider are different) and distributed services (where multiple service providers each authorize a piece of the request). Complex scenarios may mix sequences, use proxy brokers, or require conditional authorization and revocation of earlier decisions.
sections.eli5: There are three main ways to ask for permission: the service equipment can ask the decision-maker on behalf of you, you can send the equipment to ask, or you can get a permission ticket first and show it later. Each way works in different situations.

sections.title: Policy and Authorization
sections.content:
Authorization decisions are often the result of evaluating policies, which are sets of rules stored by each organization. A policy for a user might say 'allow access only during business hours' or for a service might say 'allow maximum 5 concurrent sessions per user.'

Policy handling involves three steps: retrieval (finding the relevant policy rules), evaluation (checking whether the request satisfies those rules), and enforcement (having the service equipment apply the decision). In a distributed authorization, each organization may retrieve, evaluate, and enforce its own policies. Policy information may also come from multiple sources: some information (like current time) may be available only at the user's home organization, while other information (like current network resource availability) may only be known to the service provider.

The framework introduces terminology from the Policy Framework working group: a Policy Retrieval Point (PRP) finds policies, a Policy Decision Point (PDP) evaluates them, Policy Information Points (PIPs) provide data needed for evaluation, and Policy Enforcement Points (PEPs) apply decisions. In multi-domain authorization, these roles may be spread across user, home organization, and service provider.
sections.eli5: Authorization rules (policies) say what you can and cannot do. Someone has to find the rules, someone has to check if your request matches them, and someone has to make sure you follow the decision. In big organizations, different people handle each of these steps.

sections.title: Attribute Certificates and Secure Transport
sections.content:
The framework describes how attribute certificates can securely carry authorization information. Unlike public key certificates, which prove 'who you are,' attribute certificates prove 'what you are allowed to do' (roles, group memberships, clearances). The analogy used in the RFC: a public key certificate is like a passport proving who you are, while an attribute certificate is like a visa stating what you are permitted to do.

ACs are digitally signed structures issued by a certificate authority (often different from the authority that issued your identity certificate). An AC contains attributes such as group membership, role, or account limits. When making an access decision, a service equipment may verify that the AC owner matches the authenticated user, typically by checking that the AC references the user's public key certificate and that the same key signed the current request.

The framework shows several architectural patterns for ACs: a client may push an AC directly to a server without new domain connections, or a server may request the client's AC from an issuer or repository after the client authenticates. Directory services such as LDAP may be used to retrieve ACs, and both client acquisition and server lookup protocols must be defined.
sections.eli5: Instead of checking 'who are you' every time, the system can use special certificates that say 'this person is allowed to do X.' These are signed so they cannot be forged, and they can be handed around so the service equipment does not have to ask your home organization every time.
